claim: Exocytosis of secretory vesicles requires the soluble N-ethylmaleimide-sensitive factor attachment protein receptor (SNARE) proteins and small GTPase Rabs.
source: Exocytosis of secretory vesicles requires the soluble N-ethylmaleimide-sensitive factor attachment protein receptor (SNARE) proteins and small GTPase Rabs.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the molecular machinery of exocytosis.

claim: Rabphilin 3A is a Rab3/Rab27 effector protein on secretory vesicles.
source: As a Rab3/Rab27 effector protein on secretory vesicles, Rabphilin 3A was implicated to interact with SNAP-25 to regulate vesicle exocytosis in neurons and neuroendocrine cells, yet the underlying mechanism remains unclear.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Rabphilin 3A's classification and localization.

claim: Rabphilin 3A was implicated to interact with SNAP-25 to regulate vesicle exocytosis in neurons and neuroendocrine cells.
source: As a Rab3/Rab27 effector protein on secretory vesicles, Rabphilin 3A was implicated to interact with SNAP-25 to regulate vesicle exocytosis in neurons and neuroendocrine cells, yet the underlying mechanism remains unclear.
evidence: This statement references prior work suggesting this interaction, though the mechanism was unclear.

claim: The underlying mechanism of how Rabphilin 3A interacts with SNAP-25 to regulate vesicle exocytosis remains unclear.
source: As a Rab3/Rab27 effector protein on secretory vesicles, Rabphilin 3A was implicated to interact with SNAP-25 to regulate vesicle exocytosis in neurons and neuroendocrine cells, yet the underlying mechanism remains unclear.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in knowledge that the study addresses.

claim: An intramolecular interplay between the N-terminal Rab-binding domain and C-terminal C2AB domain enables Rabphilin 3A to strongly bind the SNAP-25 N-peptide region via its C2B bottom α-helix.
source: We found that an intramolecular interplay between the N-terminal Rab-binding domain and C-terminal C2AB domain enables Rabphilin 3A to strongly bind the SNAP-25 N-peptide region via its C2B bottom α-helix.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Disruption of the Rabphilin 3A-SNAP-25 interaction significantly impaired docking and fusion of vesicles with the plasma membrane in rat PC12 cells.
source: Disruption of this interaction significantly impaired docking and fusion of vesicles with the plasma membrane in rat PC12 cells.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data in PC12 cells shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: The Rabphilin 3A-SNAP-25 interaction allows Rabphilin 3A to accelerate SNARE complex assembly.
source: In addition, we found that this interaction allows Rabphilin 3A to accelerate SNARE complex assembly.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by FRET assay data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The Rabphilin 3A-SNAP-25 interaction accelerates SNARE complex assembly via inducing a conformational switch from random coils to α-helical structure in the SNAP-25 SNARE motif.
source: Furthermore, we revealed that this interaction accelerates SNARE complex assembly via inducing a conformational switch from random coils to α-helical structure in the SNAP-25 SNARE motif.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by bimane-tryptophan quenching assay data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The promotion of SNARE complex assembly by binding the C2B bottom α-helix of Rabphilin 3A to the N-peptide of SNAP-25 underlies a pre-fusion function of Rabphilin 3A in vesicle exocytosis.
source: Altogether, our data suggest that the promotion of SNARE complex assembly by binding the C2B bottom α-helix of Rabphilin 3A to the N-peptide of SNAP-25 underlies a pre-fusion function of Rabphilin 3A in vesicle exocytosis.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, integrating multiple experimental findings.

claim: Secretion of neurotransmitters and hormones mediated by Ca2+-regulated exocytosis in neurons and neuroendocrine cells is achieved by a series of intracellular membrane trafficking steps, including recruitment, docking, priming, and fusion of secretory vesicles with the plasma membrane.
source: Secretion of neurotransmitters and hormones mediated by Ca2+-regulated exocytosis in neurons and neuroendocrine cells is achieved by a series of intracellular membrane trafficking steps, including recruitment, docking, priming, and fusion of secretory vesicles with the plasma membrane (Rettig and Neher, 2002; Südhof and Rizo, 2011; Jahn and Fasshauer, 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge about exocytosis, supported by citations.

claim: The core machinery governing the exocytosis process involves the SNARE proteins synaptobrevin-2 (Syb2) on secretory vesicles, and syntaxin-1 (Syx1) and SNAP-25 (SN25) on the plasma membrane.
source: The core machinery governing the process involves the SNARE proteins synaptobrevin-2 (Syb2) on secretory vesicles, and syntaxin-1 (Syx1) and SNAP-25 (SN25) on the plasma membrane, which form the four helical bundle structure called the SNARE complex to bring the two membranes into close proximity and eventually drive membrane fusion (Jahn and Scheller, 2006; Sutton et al., 1998; Weber et al., 1998).
evidence: This is established knowledge about SNARE proteins, supported by citations.

claim: SNARE proteins form the four helical bundle structure called the SNARE complex to bring the two membranes into close proximity and eventually drive membrane fusion.
source: The core machinery governing the process involves the SNARE proteins synaptobrevin-2 (Syb2) on secretory vesicles, and syntaxin-1 (Syx1) and SNAP-25 (SN25) on the plasma membrane, which form the four helical bundle structure called the SNARE complex to bring the two membranes into close proximity and eventually drive membrane fusion (Jahn and Scheller, 2006; Sutton et al., 1998; Weber et al., 1998).
evidence: This is established knowledge about SNARE complex function, supported by citations.

claim: Small GTPase Rabs are essential regulators in the secretory pathway, which have specific role in defining the identity of subcellular membranes.
source: Small GTPase Rabs are essential regulators in the secretory pathway, which have specific role in defining the identity of subcellular membranes (Stenmark, 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Rab proteins, supported by citation.

claim: Rab3A and Rab27A are abundantly expressed in neurons and neuroendocrine cells and associate with the membrane of secretory vesicles in a GTP-bound form to regulate vesicle exocytosis.
source: Rab3A and Rab27A are abundantly expressed in neurons and neuroendocrine cells and associate with the membrane of secretory vesicles in a GTP-bound form to regulate vesicle exocytosis (Takai et al., 1996; Geppert and Südhof, 1998; Fukuda, 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Rab3A and Rab27A, supported by citations.

claim: Rabphilin 3A (Rph3A) was originally identified as a GTP-Rab3A-binding protein and found to regulate SNARE-dependent exocytosis.
source: Rabphilin 3A (Rph3A) was originally identified as a GTP-Rab3A-binding protein and found to regulate SNARE-dependent exocytosis (Shirataki et al., 1992; Tsuboi and Fukuda, 2005; Deák et al., 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Rph3A, supported by citations.

claim: Loss of Rph3A is associated with Alzheimer's and Huntington's disease.
source: Recent studies have found that loss of Rph3A is associated with Alzheimer's and Huntington's disease, suggesting a crucial role of Rph3A in synaptic function (Smith et al., 2005; Smith et al., 2007; Tan et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies linking Rph3A loss to neurodegenerative diseases.

claim: Loss of Rph3A suggests a crucial role of Rph3A in synaptic function.
source: Recent studies have found that loss of Rph3A is associated with Alzheimer's and Huntington's disease, suggesting a crucial role of Rph3A in synaptic function (Smith et al., 2005; Smith et al., 2007; Tan et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the association of Rph3A loss with disease, supported by citations.

claim: Rph3A contains an N-terminal Rab-binding domain (RBD) that associates with secretory vesicles via binding to GTP-bound Rab3A or Rab27A.
source: Rph3A contains an N-terminal Rab-binding domain (RBD) that associates with secretory vesicles via binding to GTP-bound Rab3A or Rab27A (Li et al., 1994; Mizoguchi et al., 1994; Fukuda et al., 2004), a proline-rich linker (PRL) region bearing multiple phosphorylation sites (Foletti et al., 2001), and two C-terminal C2 domains (termed C2A and C2B, respectively) that interact with phospholipids and the SNAREs (Yamaguchi et al., 1993; Chung et al., 1998; Tsuboi and Fukuda, 2005; Figure 1A).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Rph3A domain structure, supported by citations and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Rph3A contains a proline-rich linker (PRL) region bearing multiple phosphorylation sites.
source: Rph3A contains an N-terminal Rab-binding domain (RBD) that associates with secretory vesicles via binding to GTP-bound Rab3A or Rab27A (Li et al., 1994; Mizoguchi et al., 1994; Fukuda et al., 2004), a proline-rich linker (PRL) region bearing multiple phosphorylation sites (Foletti et al., 2001), and two C-terminal C2 domains (termed C2A and C2B, respectively) that interact with phospholipids and the SNAREs (Yamaguchi et al., 1993; Chung et al., 1998; Tsuboi and Fukuda, 2005; Figure 1A).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Rph3A domain structure, supported by citations and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Rph3A contains two C-terminal C2 domains (termed C2A and C2B, respectively) that interact with phospholipids and the SNAREs.
source: Rph3A contains an N-terminal Rab-binding domain (RBD) that associates with secretory vesicles via binding to GTP-bound Rab3A or Rab27A (Li et al., 1994; Mizoguchi et al., 1994; Fukuda et al., 2004), a proline-rich linker (PRL) region bearing multiple phosphorylation sites (Foletti et al., 2001), and two C-terminal C2 domains (termed C2A and C2B, respectively) that interact with phospholipids and the SNAREs (Yamaguchi et al., 1993; Chung et al., 1998; Tsuboi and Fukuda, 2005; Figure 1A).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Rph3A domain structure, supported by citations and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: The C2B domain of Rph3A binds SN25 to regulate exocytosis of dense-core vesicles (DCVs) in PC12 cells and fine-tune re-priming of synaptic vesicles in hippocampal neurons.
source: In particular, increasing evidence showed that the C2B domain of Rph3A binds SN25 to regulate exocytosis of dense-core vesicles (DCVs) in PC12 cells and fine-tune re-priming of synaptic vesicles in hippocampal neurons (Tsuboi and Fukuda, 2005; Deák et al., 2006), but the underlying mechanism was unclear.
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior studies, supported by citations.

claim: The underlying mechanism of how the C2B domain of Rph3A binds SN25 to regulate exocytosis was unclear.
source: In particular, increasing evidence showed that the C2B domain of Rph3A binds SN25 to regulate exocytosis of dense-core vesicles (DCVs) in PC12 cells and fine-tune re-priming of synaptic vesicles in hippocampal neurons (Tsuboi and Fukuda, 2005; Deák et al., 2006), but the underlying mechanism was unclear.
evidence: This identifies a gap in knowledge that the study addresses.

claim: It was previously reported that Rph3A binds SN25 via the β3-β4 polybasic region of the C2B domain.
source: It was previously reported that Rph3A binds SN25 via the β3-β4 polybasic region of the C2B domain (Tsuboi et al., 2007), while later structural results identified that Rph3A interacts with SN25 via the α-helix at the bottom face of the C2B domain (Deák et al., 2006; Ferrer-Orta et al., 2017).
evidence: This is prior knowledge from a cited study.

claim: Later structural results identified that Rph3A interacts with SN25 via the α-helix at the bottom face of the C2B domain.
source: It was previously reported that Rph3A binds SN25 via the β3-β4 polybasic region of the C2B domain (Tsuboi et al., 2007), while later structural results identified that Rph3A interacts with SN25 via the α-helix at the bottom face of the C2B domain (Deák et al., 2006; Ferrer-Orta et al., 2017).
evidence: This is prior knowledge from cited structural studies.

claim: According to the crystal structure of the Rph3A-C2B–SN25 complex, three distinct sites in SN25 were found to participate in binding to Rph3A-C2B.
source: In addition, according to the crystal structure of the Rph3A-C2B–SN25 complex, three distinct sites in SN25 were found to participate in binding to Rph3A-C2B, two of which located in the middle region of the SNARE motif of SN25, and one resided at the N-terminus of SN25 (Ferrer-Orta et al., 2017).
evidence: This is prior knowledge from a cited structural study.

claim: Two of the three distinct sites in SN25 that participate in binding to Rph3A-C2B are located in the middle region of the SNARE motif of SN25.
source: In addition, according to the crystal structure of the Rph3A-C2B–SN25 complex, three distinct sites in SN25 were found to participate in binding to Rph3A-C2B, two of which located in the middle region of the SNARE motif of SN25, and one resided at the N-terminus of SN25 (Ferrer-Orta et al., 2017).
evidence: This is prior knowledge from a cited structural study.

claim: One of the three distinct sites in SN25 that participate in binding to Rph3A-C2B resides at the N-terminus of SN25.
source: In addition, according to the crystal structure of the Rph3A-C2B–SN25 complex, three distinct sites in SN25 were found to participate in binding to Rph3A-C2B, two of which located in the middle region of the SNARE motif of SN25, and one resided at the N-terminus of SN25 (Ferrer-Orta et al., 2017).
evidence: This is prior knowledge from a cited structural study.

claim: It remains elusive which binding mode of the Rph3A-C2B–SN25 interaction is physiologically relevant.
source: However, it remains elusive which binding mode of the Rph3A-C2B–SN25 interaction is physiologically relevant.
evidence: This identifies a gap in knowledge that the study addresses.

claim: Little is known how the Rph3A-C2B–SN25 interaction regulates vesicle exocytosis.
source: Importantly, little is known how this interaction regulates vesicle exocytosis.
evidence: This identifies a gap in knowledge that the study addresses.

claim: Rph3A FL displayed a strong tendency to form monomer in solution, as detected by size-exclusion chromatograph and analytical ultracentrifugation (AUC).
source: Rph3A FL displayed a strong tendency to form monomer in solution, as detected by size-exclusion chromatograph and analytical ultracentrifugation (AUC) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: GST alone displayed no binding to Rph3A FL and the truncations.
source: As controls, GST alone displayed no binding to Rph3A FL and the truncations.
evidence: This is a control result from GST pull-down experiments shown in Figure 1B and C.

claim: GST-SN25 showed significant interaction with Rph3A (182–681), Rph3A (282–681), and Rph3A (372–681).
source: In contrast, GST-SN25 showed significant interaction with Rph3A (182–681), Rph3A (282–681), and Rph3A (372–681), but failed to bind Rph3A (1–281) (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and C.

claim: GST-SN25 failed to bind Rph3A (1–281).
source: In contrast, GST-SN25 showed significant interaction with Rph3A (182–681), Rph3A (282–681), and Rph3A (372–681), but failed to bind Rph3A (1–281) (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and C.

claim: The C-terminal C2AB of Rph3A contributes predominately to SN25 interaction.
source: Consistent with previous observations, these data indicate that the C-terminal C2AB of Rph3A contributes predominately to SN25 interaction.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental data shown in Figure 1B and C, consistent with prior observations.

claim: GST-SN25 showed much more stronger binding capacity to Rph3A FL than to the truncations.
source: Intriguingly, GST-SN25 showed much more stronger binding capacity to Rph3A FL than to the above truncations (Figure 1B and C), and titration of Rph3A FL to GST-SN25 yielded a Kd of 3.293±0.4787 µM (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B, C, and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Titration of Rph3A FL to GST-SN25 yielded a Kd of 3.293±0.4787 µM.
source: Intriguingly, GST-SN25 showed much more stronger binding capacity to Rph3A FL than to the above truncations (Figure 1B and C), and titration of Rph3A FL to GST-SN25 yielded a Kd of 3.293±0.4787 µM (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The N-terminal region of Rph3A cooperates with the C-terminal C2AB to enhance SN25 binding.
source: As Rph3A (1–281) did not bind SN25, the only explanation is that the N-terminal region of Rph3A cooperates with the C-terminal C2AB to enhance SN25 binding.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental data showing that full-length Rph3A binds more strongly than truncations.

claim: Both Rph3A (Δ185–371) and Rph3A (Δ1–45 and Δ161–371) bound to GST-SN25 as effectively as Rph3A FL.
source: Both variants bound to GST-SN25 as effectively as Rph3A FL (Figure 1D and E), revealing that the RBD is important for the enhanced SN25 binding.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D and E.

claim: The RBD is important for the enhanced SN25 binding.
source: Both variants bound to GST-SN25 as effectively as Rph3A FL (Figure 1D and E), revealing that the RBD is important for the enhanced SN25 binding.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental data shown in Figure 1D and E.

claim: An intramolecular interplay between the RBD and the C2AB may enhance Rph3A–SN25 binding.
source: As Rph3A FL prefers a monomeric state in solution and the RBD alone displayed no detectable binding to GST-SN25 as shown in Figure 1B and C, we suspect that an intramolecular interplay between the RBD and the C2AB may enhance Rph3A–SN25 binding.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the experimental observations.

claim: GST-tagged Rph3A-RBD (40–170) but not GST alone bound to His6-tagged Rph3A-C2AB (372–681).
source: Indeed, we observed that GST-tagged Rph3A-RBD (40–170) but not GST alone bound to His6-tagged Rph3A-C2AB (372–681), as detected by pull-down assay combined with immunoblotting (Figure 1G and H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G and H.

claim: Mutation of G102/L104 (G102A/L104A, referred to as GLAA) abolished the binding of Rph3A-RBD to Rph3A-C2AB.
source: Upon screening, we found that mutation of G102/L104 (G102A/L104A, referred to as GLAA) abolished the binding of Rph3A-RBD to Rph3A-C2AB, as detected by immunoblotting (Figure 1G and H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G and H.

claim: The GLAA mutation in Rph3A (Δ185–371) severely impaired GST-SN25 binding.
source: To confirm this, we also introduced the GLAA mutation to Rph3A (Δ185–371) and found that it severely impaired GST-SN25 binding (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A,B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A,B.

claim: A new binding mode between Rph3A and SN25 relies on an intramolecular interplay of the RBD with C2AB in Rph3A.
source: Altogether, these data suggest a new binding mode between Rph3A and SN25 which relies on an intramolecular interplay of the RBD with C2AB in Rph3A.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data in Figure 1.

claim: The RBD of Rph3A can bind Rab3A (Q81L, GTP-bound form).
source: The RBD of Rph3A can bind Rab3A (Q81L, GTP-bound form) as well (Stahl et al., 1996; Ostermeier and Brunger, 1999).
evidence: This is established knowledge from cited studies.

claim: The binding sites for Rab3A position away from residues G102/L104 in the RBD.
source: Based on the crystal structure of the Rph3A-RBD–Rab3A complex (Ostermeier and Brunger, 1999), the binding sites for Rab3A position away from residues G102/L104 in the RBD (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C), suggesting that the intramolecular interplay of the RBD with C2AB might be compatible with Rab3A interaction.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis of a cited crystal structure, shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3C.

claim: The intramolecular interplay of the RBD with C2AB might be compatible with Rab3A interaction.
source: Based on the crystal structure of the Rph3A-RBD–Rab3A complex (Ostermeier and Brunger, 1999), the binding sites for Rab3A position away from residues G102/L104 in the RBD (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C), suggesting that the intramolecular interplay of the RBD with C2AB might be compatible with Rab3A interaction.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on structural analysis.

claim: The involvement of Rab3A did not influence the strong interaction between GST-SN25 and Rph3A FL mediated by the intramolecular interplay of the RBD with C2AB.
source: Indeed, pull-down experiments showed that the involvement of Rab3A did not influence the strong interaction between GST-SN25 and Rph3A FL mediated by the intramolecular interplay of the RBD with C2AB (Figure 1I and J).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1I and J.

claim: Rab3A showed significant binding to the Rph3A FL–SN25 complex.
source: Instead, Rab3A showed significant binding to the Rph3A FL–SN25 complex (Figure 1I and J), implying that Rph3A is able to serve as a connector to bridge vesicle-bound Rab3A and plasma membrane-bound SN25.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1I and J.

claim: Rph3A is able to serve as a connector to bridge vesicle-bound Rab3A and plasma membrane-bound SN25.
source: Instead, Rab3A showed significant binding to the Rph3A FL–SN25 complex (Figure 1I and J), implying that Rph3A is able to serve as a connector to bridge vesicle-bound Rab3A and plasma membrane-bound SN25.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental data shown in Figure 1I and J.

claim: SN25 (1–82) and SN25 (1–140) significantly bound to Rph3A FL, as effectively as SN25 FL.
source: Among these fragments, SN25 (1–82) and SN25 (1–140) significantly bound to Rph3A FL, as effectively as SN25 FL (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and C.

claim: GST alone and the other SN25 fragments failed to bind Rph3A FL.
source: In contrast, GST alone and the other SN25 fragments failed to bind Rph3A FL (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and C.

claim: Rph3A FL binds to the N-terminal region of SN25 comprising the SN1 and the N-peptide.
source: Hence, these data suggest that Rph3A FL binds to the N-terminal region of SN25 comprising the SN1 and the N-peptide.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental data shown in Figure 2B and C.

claim: GST-SN25 (7–82) strongly impaired Rph3A FL binding.
source: To our surprise, in contrast to the strong interaction of GST-SN25 (1–82) with Rph3A FL, GST-SN25 (7–82) strongly impaired Rph3A FL binding, and GST-SN25 (11–82) failed to bind Rph3A FL (Figure 2E and F), showing that the N-peptide sequence (1MAEDADMRNE10) is essential for mediating binding of SN25 to Rph3A FL.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E and F.

claim: GST-SN25 (11–82) failed to bind Rph3A FL.
source: To our surprise, in contrast to the strong interaction of GST-SN25 (1–82) with Rph3A FL, GST-SN25 (7–82) strongly impaired Rph3A FL binding, and GST-SN25 (11–82) failed to bind Rph3A FL (Figure 2E and F), showing that the N-peptide sequence (1MAEDADMRNE10) is essential for mediating binding of SN25 to Rph3A FL.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E and F.

claim: The N-peptide sequence (1MAEDADMRNE10) is essential for mediating binding of SN25 to Rph3A FL.
source: To our surprise, in contrast to the strong interaction of GST-SN25 (1–82) with Rph3A FL, GST-SN25 (7–82) strongly impaired Rph3A FL binding, and GST-SN25 (11–82) failed to bind Rph3A FL (Figure 2E and F), showing that the N-peptide sequence (1MAEDADMRNE10) is essential for mediating binding of SN25 to Rph3A FL.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data shown in Figure 2E and F.

claim: The SN25 (1–82) EDR mutant (E38A/D41A/R45A) retained strong binding to Rph3A FL.
source: To figure this out, we made an SN25 (1–82) mutant which carries E38A/D41A/R45A (EDR) and examined its interaction with Rph3A FL. Similar to SN25 (1–82), the EDR mutant retained strong binding to Rph3A FL (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), suggesting that the N-peptide rather than the SN1 mediates Rph3A FL interaction.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The N-peptide rather than the SN1 mediates Rph3A FL interaction.
source: To figure this out, we made an SN25 (1–82) mutant which carries E38A/D41A/R45A (EDR) and examined its interaction with Rph3A FL. Similar to SN25 (1–82), the EDR mutant retained strong binding to Rph3A FL (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), suggesting that the N-peptide rather than the SN1 mediates Rph3A FL interaction.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The binding mode between Rph3A FL and SN25 is distinct from the mode between Rph3A-C2B and SN25.
source: Taken together, these data indicate that the binding mode between Rph3A FL and SN25 is distinct from the mode between Rph3A-C2B and SN25, in line with the results shown in Figure 1.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data in Figure 2.

claim: The negatively charged N-peptide sequence of SN25 is conserved among different species.
source: In addition, sequence alignment showed that the negatively charged N-peptide sequence of SN25 is conserved among different species (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The N-peptide sequence of SN25 is not conserved in other isoforms such as SNAP-23, SNAP-47, SNAP-29, and Qb SNAREs (e.g., Vti1A, Vti1B, GOSR1, GOSR2, and Sec20).
source: However, the N-peptide sequence of SN25 is not conserved in other isoforms such as SNAP-23, SNAP-47, SNAP-29, and Qb SNAREs (e.g., Vti1A, Vti1B, GOSR1, GOSR2, and Sec20) (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B,C).
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B,C.

claim: The D4A mutation significantly impaired binding of SN25 (1–82) to Rph3A FL.
source: To identify the key residues in the sequence that mediates Rph3A interaction, we introduced the E3A, D4A, and D6A single mutation to SN25 (1–82), and found that the D4A mutation significantly impaired binding of SN25 (1–82) to Rph3A FL (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Deletion of the N-peptide of SN25 (11–206) remarkably impaired binding to Rph3A FL in the presence of negative membranes.
source: Moreover, we verified this binding modality in the presence of liposomes with physiological lipid composition, we performed lipid sedimentation assay and found that compared to SN25 (1–206), deletion of the N-peptide of SN25 (11–206) remarkably impaired binding to Rph3A FL in the presence of negative membranes (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: SN25 N-peptide mediates Rph3A FL interaction.
source: Altogether, these results show that SN25 N-peptide mediates Rph3A FL interaction.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data in Figure 2 and supplements.

claim: Rph3A regulates exocytosis of DCV in neuroendocrine cells.
source: It was previously reported that Rph3A regulates exocytosis of DCV in neuroendocrine cells (Tsuboi and Fukuda, 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge from a cited study.

claim: SN25 knockdown cells showed significantly reduced number of plasma membrane-docked DCVs, in comparison with control cells.
source: As expected, SN25 knockdown cells showed significantly reduced number of plasma membrane-docked DCVs, in comparison with control cells (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B and C.

claim: Expression of SN25 (full length, 1–206) restored the number of docked DCVs.
source: Expression of SN25 (full length, 1–206) restored the number of docked DCVs, whereas the expression of the SN25 mutant (11–206) that lacks the N-peptide exhibited strongly impaired ability to restore the docked DCVs in PC12 cells (Figure 3B and C), revealing that the N-peptide of SN25 is required for DCV docking.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B and C.

claim: Expression of the SN25 mutant (11–206) that lacks the N-peptide exhibited strongly impaired ability to restore the docked DCVs in PC12 cells.
source: Expression of SN25 (full length, 1–206) restored the number of docked DCVs, whereas the expression of the SN25 mutant (11–206) that lacks the N-peptide exhibited strongly impaired ability to restore the docked DCVs in PC12 cells (Figure 3B and C), revealing that the N-peptide of SN25 is required for DCV docking.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B and C.

claim: The N-peptide of SN25 is required for DCV docking.
source: Expression of SN25 (full length, 1–206) restored the number of docked DCVs, whereas the expression of the SN25 mutant (11–206) that lacks the N-peptide exhibited strongly impaired ability to restore the docked DCVs in PC12 cells (Figure 3B and C), revealing that the N-peptide of SN25 is required for DCV docking.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data shown in Figure 3B and C.

claim: The total number of release events in SN25 knockdown cells was significantly fewer than that in control cells.
source: The total number of release events in SN25 knockdown cells was significantly fewer than that in control cells (Figure 3D and E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D and E.

claim: Addition of Syx1 and Syb2 to SN25 E55W/R59C led to further reduced bimane fluorescence.

claim: The conformational change of SN1 from random coils to α-helix is driven by the formation of the SNARE complex.
source: As a positive control, addition of Syx1 and Syb2 to SN25 E55W/R59C led to further reduced bimane fluorescence (Figure 6B and C), consistent with the conformational change of SN1 (from random coils to α-helix) driven by the formation of the SNARE complex (Sutton et al., 1998).
evidence: This is established knowledge from a cited study, consistent with the experimental data shown in Figure 6B and C.

claim: Conformational change of SN1 can be detected by using the bimane-tryptophan quenching assay.

evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B and C.

claim: The C2B bottom α-helix of Rph3A is required for inducing conformational change of SN1.

evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data shown in Figure 6B and C.

claim: Rph3A FL promotes SNARE complex assembly via inducing the conformational change of SN1 from random coil to α-helix, and the promotion requires the interaction of the C2B bottom α-helix of Rph3A with the N-peptide of SN25.

claim: Rph3A has at least two important roles in prefusion events of exocytosis: one is to promote vesicle docking dependent on its associations with Rab3A and SN25 between the two opposite membranes; the other is to promote vesicle priming via accelerating SNARE complex assembly.
source: Taken together, we suggest that Rph3A has at least two important roles in prefusion events of exocytosis: one is to promote vesicle docking dependent on its associations with Rab3A and SN25 between the two opposite membranes; the other is to promote vesicle priming via accelerating SNARE complex assembly (Figure 7).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data throughout the study, illustrated in Figure 7.

claim: The N-peptide of Syx1 bound to Munc18-1 plays a regulatory role in exocytosis.
source: Previous studies have revealed that the N-peptide of Syx1 bound to Munc18-1 plays a regulatory role in exocytosis and that the N-terminal proline-rich sequence of Syb2 bound to intersectin-1 is necessary for the clearance of SNARE complexes required for vesicle recycling (Rathore et al., 2010; Jäpel et al., 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge from cited studies.

claim: The N-terminal proline-rich sequence of Syb2 bound to intersectin-1 is necessary for the clearance of SNARE complexes required for vesicle recycling.

evidence: This is established knowledge from cited studies.

claim: In isolated form, the SNARE motifs of Syx1, SN25, and Syb2 all assume unstructured conformation.
source: In isolated form, the SNARE motifs of Syx1, SN25, and Syb2 all assume unstructured conformation (Fasshauer et al., 1997; Hazzard et al., 1999).

claim: In the crystal structures of Munc18-1 bound to Syb2 or Syx1 and of Vps33 bound to Nyv1 or Vam3, the SNARE motifs of Syb2 or Syx1, and Nyv1 or Vam3 display highly ordered α-helical structures.
source: However, as observed in the crystal structures of Munc18-1 bound to Syb2 or Syx1 and of Vps33 bound to Nyv1 or Vam3, the SNARE motifs of Syb2 or Syx1, and Nyv1 or Vam3 display highly ordered α-helical structures (Baker et al., 2015; Stepien et al., 2022), resemblance to their conformations in the assembled SNARE complex, suggesting that the prestructured SNARE motif of the SNAREs might be essential for proper SNARE pairing and register.
evidence: This is established knowledge from cited structural studies.

claim: The prestructured SNARE motif of the SNAREs might be essential for proper SNARE pairing and register.

claim: Rph3A bound to SN25 renders SN1 to assume a prestructured conformation.

claim: Rph3A loss has almost no phenotype in mammalian neurons.

source: It is of note that the synapse has evolved a number of specialized sites beneath the presynaptic membrane (active zones) opposing the postsynaptic density, which are composed of multiple active-zone components required for synaptic vesicle exocytosis.

claim: Active-zone components may take the place of Rph3A in tethering/docking vesicles at the release sites and priming them for fusion.
source: Such active-zone components may take the place of Rph3A in tethering/docking vesicles at the release sites and priming them for fusion.
evidence: This is a hypothesis to explain the lack of phenotype in neurons upon Rph3A loss.

source: However, neuroendocrine cells lack compartmentalized active zones on the plasma membrane, in which RIMs, Munc13, CAPS, and so forth, are dominantly distributed in the cytosol instead of the plasma membrane (Fukuda, 2004; Kabachinski et al., 2014; Kabachinski et al., 2016; Houy et al., 2022), rendering them unlikely to compensate the loss of Rph3A in DCV exocytosis.
evidence: This is an inference based on the localization of these proteins in neuroendocrine cells.
